abstract.t: This document is the PIC Prover and Verifier Specification, a subordinate specification of the PIC Specification. It defines the normative requirements for the two complementary components of continuity handling:

list.t: PIC Provers: the components that construct candidate continuity advancements and the evidence required by the selected profile;
PIC Verifiers: the trusted components that validate those advancements and enforce the invariants claimed by the selected profile at verification time.

abstract.t: At every hop, a node can act in both roles: it verifies the continuity state received from its predecessor and proposes the next continuity advancement required by the selected profile. A profile may call the accepted result a Proof of Continuity only to the extent that its concrete acceptance predicate is shown to refine the abstract PoR and non-expansion predicates of the PIC Model.

It specifies the logical objects, per-hop Proof of Relationship, and continuity-advancement requirements (Section 2), the ordered Verifier checks - including profile-conditional request/execution binding - that validate a hop before authority is exercised (Section 3), authority as an abstract attenuation domain with a Policy Decision Point boundary (Section 4), and profile-selected continuity representations (Section 5).
This document does not redefine, extend, or alter the PIC Model or the normative semantics defined by the PIC Specification.
In case of conflict, the PIC Specification is authoritative.

section.name: Introduction
section.t: This section is non-normative. It describes the problem this specification addresses and is independent of any concrete implementation. Normative requirements are defined in Prover Requirements, Verifier Requirements, Authority Domains and Attenuation Profiles, and Security Considerations, together with the requirements explicitly identified in Continuity Representations. The status of a requirement does not depend on section numbering.

Current authorization models lack a formal execution continuity model: they define who may hold authority, but not how authority remains valid across the steps of a distributed execution. This specification defines how the Provenance Identity Continuity (PIC) Model is implemented at each execution hop to close that gap. The model, including Proof of Relationship (PoR), Proof of Continuity (PoC), and the resulting safety guarantees, is formally defined in the companion paper [1] and formally verified with the Lean theorem prover [2]. The paper treats PoR as an abstract, unforgeable primitive. A concrete profile realizes the full model only when it defines evidence and a receiving predicate that soundly witness that primitive. This document specifies the two components that process such evidence:

The earlier authority-propagation analysis records the transition from possession-based reasoning to continuity-based reasoning and its application to the confused-deputy problem [15]. Later relational and event-level results refine the realization boundary without changing the core non-expansion invariant [13] [14].

list.t: The PIC Prover constructs the relationship or profile evidence required by the selected profile and uses it to construct a candidate advancement handed to the next verification boundary.

The PIC Verifier validates the candidate at the receiving hop. For a full-continuity profile, it validates concrete evidence that soundly witnesses the abstract PoR together with non-expansion and all other profile checks. For an artifact-linked profile, it validates only the narrower artifact, key, authority, and contract relationships the profile defines.

section.t: These assurance levels are not interchangeable. In particular, a signed predecessor, an executor-profile credential, possession of a workload key, and a non-expansive authority transition do not by themselves prove that a trusted boundary observed the concrete handoff or request occurrence that caused the successor action.

PIC does not require a central server. Depending on deployment topology and selected profile, a chain can be validated fully decentralized — each hop carrying everything the next needs to verify it — or with the help of a trusted component such as a snapshot server. Section 5 describes these representations; the PIC invariants are the same in every case, but the concrete assurance and trust assumptions differ by profile (see Incremental Verification and Trusted Hops and Deployment Models) — the profiles are not equivalent.

This statement concerns the abstract PIC model and profile space. An interoperable profile may select centralized settlement, decentralized validation, authenticated checkpoints, full history, or another representation. No product, service, deployment topology, or wire encoding is required by the abstract PIC model. A profile that establishes only signed predecessor linkage, key binding, authority attenuation, and execution-contract conformance has an artifact-linked assurance level; it does not thereby establish observed-handoff PoR, request binding, complete mediation, or causal attribution of a runtime action.

PIC also draws a clean line between the security model and transport. The guarantees come from the signed continuity chain, not from how it travels: an implementation must not rely on the transport — a TLS session, a network perimeter, a message bus — to obtain them (the normative requirement is stated in Section 7.7). Transport is only transport. A compromised channel can read or drop messages but cannot forge a valid PCA; confidentiality and attack-surface concerns belong to transport and are addressed in Section 7.7. This separation is what lets the same model run unchanged over HTTP, over messaging systems such as Apache Kafka, or over any other carrier.

section.name: Security Guarantees of the Model
section.t: An authority-propagation protocol guarantees the validity of authority states, not the physical behavior of executors. PIC guarantees that no actor can cause a conforming executor to accept or propagate an invalid authority state as valid PIC state: an operation is accepted only if it can be represented as a valid continuation of the authority carried by the request.

Physical behavior is outside this guarantee, for PIC as for any security protocol. No authorization model can guarantee that an application is free of bugs or that an executor behaves correctly: an executor that receives authority to READ, ignores it, and physically performs DELETE fails as an implementation, locally. What the protocol guarantees is that such a fault remains local: executor n+1 cannot continue, as valid, an authority state that the model defines as invalid.

The same applies to the cryptographic assumptions. Capability and token systems, such as OAuth, rest on the unforgeability of their credentials: if the underlying cryptography is broken, none of their properties survive. PIC rests on the same cryptographic assumptions, and so does the Proof of Relationship: the relationship evidence is assumed unforgeable, and a break of the underlying cryptography is outside the model, as it is for every protocol in this space.

This boundary is what distinguishes PIC. If authority from two independent lineages can be composed into a new state that remains valid under a model, that model relies on correct executor behavior to avoid the composition. Under PIC such a mixed state is invalid by construction: the damage of a buggy or compromised executor is confined to its local step and cannot propagate as valid authority at the next hop.

section.name: Delegating the Future
section.t: Software that must support implementations that do not exist yet does not hard-code future components. It defines an interface. The interface specifies the contract, and any future implementation can participate, provided it proves that it satisfies the contract.
PIC applies the same principle to distributed execution. A continuation does not name or preselect its successor. It defines the execution contract instead:

list.t: the authority that may continue;
the constraints that must remain non-expansive;
the execution characteristics the successor must satisfy;
the causal relationship with the previous execution state.

section.t: When a successor materializes, it proves that it satisfies those conditions and may continue the execution. No identity needs to be known in advance, and nothing binds the contract to a single successor: a continuation may be taken up by zero, one, or many executors, possibly in parallel. The future being delegated ranges from no continuation at all to an unbounded number of them. Identity may still support authentication, audit, and accountability, but it is not the primitive that preserves authority across execution.
The contract defines the continuation. The executor proves conformance. Continuity, not identity, delegates the future.

section.name: The N+1 Executor Problem (Canonical Execution Model)
section.t: The N+1 Executor Problem is future delegation made concrete. This specification is explained and defined around this single canonical execution model. Execution is a chain of discrete steps performed by executors, such as services, workloads, functions, tools, or agents. Each executor receives a request, processes it, and may cause a further step:

Each | marks a hop boundary: the point where the predecessor's Prover emits its proofs and the successor's Verifier validates them. Each boundary is an act of future delegation, and the linear chain is the minimal case: a step may delegate to several successors in parallel.

The problem is the executor at position n+1. Executor n acts at time x. Executor n+1 acts at a later time x + y, and at time x it does not yet exist as a known party: it need not be known, selected, instantiated, or provisioned when executor n completes its step. Consequently, no security mechanism that requires pre-binding authority to a concrete successor (its identity, its key, or its channel) can be applied at time x: there is no holder yet to bind to.

The problem does not require a long chain: it already holds for n = 0. The first hop, from the origin that expresses an intent to the first executor that serves it, crosses the same temporal gap, since that executor too may not exist or be known at the time the intent is expressed. A single-hop execution is the smallest instance of the N+1 Executor Problem. Multi-hop chains repeat it at every boundary, where its consequences become most visible.

section.name: Cross-Lineage Authority Composition
section.t: An executor may serve more than one lineage at the same time. Each lineage carries its own authority context, attenuated along its own chain. A bug, or an adversarially influenced agent, can compose authority across those lineages: a privilege carried by one lineage is attached to the continuation of another.

In a possession-based model the resulting state is valid. Every privilege presented at executor n+1 is genuinely possessed and correctly signed; nothing in the model distinguishes them by origin. The bug has created a valid security state, and READ-ALL combined with SHARE-FILES is now exercisable in a lineage that was never granted it.

Under PIC the same state cannot be represented as valid. READ-ALL is absent from the origin context of lineage B, and no valid continuation can expand an authority context: the composed proof does not satisfy the lineage, and the Verifier at executor n+1 rejects it. The bug can still execute locally, as stated in Section 1.1, but the state it produces is invalid and stops at that hop.

This document's ordinary advancement has exactly one predecessor. A future causal-DAG profile that defines an ordinary multi-parent join must preserve every parent bound; for set-valued authority, the joined authority is a subset of the intersection of the parent authorities. If a join intentionally creates a state more permissive than any parent, it is an explicit, separately authorized composition or relaxation event, not an ordinary continuation [14].

This is a structural elimination of silent cross-lineage confused-deputy authority composition from the ordinary PIC continuation model, and it is what PIC shares with the object-capability approach: a capability removes the mismatch by construction at a single hop, by fusing designation and authority at invocation; PIC extends the same by-construction guarantee across an ordinary lineage, so the mismatch is not a state a valid chain can represent at any hop. It is ruled out by construction, not caught by runtime vigilance — and this is exactly the property the Lean formalization verifies [2].

section.name: The Execution Flow as Part of the Security Model
section.t: The PIC Model resolves the N+1 Executor Problem by bringing the execution flow itself, including the not-yet-existing executor n+1, into the security model, rather than leaving the gap between x and x + y to application logic. What must hold across that gap is not the identity of the successor, but that its authority is a valid continuation of the context that caused it. The temporal gap is therefore not an application concern to be patched with perimeter assumptions or out-of-band coordination: it is the object the security model is built around, and authority crosses it only as verified continuity, never as possession by a pre-existing holder.

section.name: Attribute Attestations
section.t: To describe the model, this specification uses one illustrative construct: the signed attribute attestation. It is a document, signed by an issuer, that binds a subject to a set of attributes for a validity period. The examples in this document follow a single running scenario: a backup service operating in the European region under compliance constraints, authorized for the operations READ-ALL and BACKUP.

figure.sourcecode: { "subject": "did:example:workloads:eu:backup-service", "attributes": { "role": "backup-service", "compliance": ["GDPR"], "accountableParty": "Example Corp", "serviceAgreements": [ "https://legal.example.com/agreements/dpa-2026-001" ], "environment": "production", "region": "eu-1", "availabilityZone": "eu-1a", "executionModel": "deterministic" }, "issuedAt": "2026-07-17T10:00:00Z", "expiresAt": "2026-08-17T10:00:00Z", "issuer": "did:example:org-authority" }

section.t: The scenario includes a second executor: a summary service implemented as an AI agent. It produces summaries of documents, and its execution is not deterministic. Its attestation differs in role, accountable party, network placement, and execution model:

figure.sourcecode: { "subject": "did:example:workloads:eu:summary-service", "attributes": { "role": "summary-service", "compliance": ["GDPR"], "accountableParty": "Acme AI Ltd", "serviceAgreements": [ "https://legal.acme.example/agreements/asa-2026-042" ], "environment": "production", "region": "eu-1", "availabilityZone": "eu-1b", "executionModel": "agentic" }, "issuedAt": "2026-07-17T10:00:00Z", "expiresAt": "2026-08-17T10:00:00Z", "issuer": "did:example:org-authority" }

section.t: The identifiers in the examples use DIDs, but this is a presentational choice, not a requirement. PIC does not depend on any identifier scheme; what it needs are the signed attestations themselves. A bare public/private key pair, with no identifier at all, is enough to sign and verify them. An identifier such as a DID only makes the examples easier to read and to cross-reference: it helps the specification, it is not necessary for the model.

For the same reason, this document deliberately does not use Verifiable Credentials, X.509 certificates, or similar formats. They would work, but understanding them is not required to understand PIC, and depending on them would tie the model to a particular identity technology. The specification uses a plain signed attestation on purpose — a minimalist approach that keeps it accessible and free of unnecessary prerequisites.

section.name: Requirements Notation
section.t: The normative sections of this document are Prover Requirements, Verifier Requirements, Authority Domains and Attenuation Profiles, and Security Considerations, together with the requirements explicitly identified in Continuity Representations. Introduction, Origins, Authorship, and Historical Record, Deployment Models, Zero Trust, Privacy Considerations, and Registry Considerations are non-normative unless a statement explicitly says otherwise.

The key words "MUST", "MUST NOT", "REQUIRED", "SHALL", "SHALL NOT", "SHOULD", "SHOULD NOT", "RECOMMENDED", "NOT RECOMMENDED", "MAY", and "OPTIONAL" in this document are to be interpreted as described in BCP 14 [3] [4] when, and only when, they appear in all capitals within normative text.
Examples in this document are illustrative and non-normative.

section.name: Origin Authority Context
section.t: A lineage begins when a principal expresses an intent within its privileges. The result is a PIC Context of Authority (PCA): the logical authority context that establishes the upper bound for the lineage. The root PCA contains no Proof of Relationship: there is no predecessor to relate to. Every later continuity advancement continues, and may only attenuate, the authority established by the root.

This specification does not require every hop to create a new signed PCA. A profile defines the concrete signed root representation and the concrete continuity-advancement representation. In PIC Profile 0.2, a PCA is serialized and signed as a native PIC PCA COSE checkpoint. A settled PIC Token JWT carries a settled PIC Continuity COSE in pic.root; the settled Continuity carries the exact signed PIC PCA COSE bytes for the current trusted checkpoint. A workload proposes one centralized advancement by signing a PIC Continuity Transition COSE, placing it in a workload-signed candidate PIC Continuity COSE, and carrying that candidate in a workload-signed candidate PIC Token JWT. The trusted settlement authority validates the candidate and issues the next settled PIC Token JWT.

The examples represent authority as an operations set — the reference profile, matching the operation-resource privileges of the model [1]. PIC does not require this representation, nor does it define the application's authorization vocabulary; Section 4 covers authority as an abstract domain (roles, labels, scopes, policy references) and its relationship to a Policy Decision Point.

The following root-PCA examples are illustrative views of a generic example profile, not the PIC Profile 0.2 logical PCA or wire schema. In particular, the illustrative continuation.mode = "single-use" member is not a Profile 0.2 field or invariant.

In the running scenario, Alice connects to the backup SaaS. The service agreement confirms that the service is operated in Europe by an accountable party and does not use agentic execution. On those terms she grants access to all her files for backup. Her client produces a root PCA, signed or otherwise authenticated by the selected origin profile:

Later, Alice uses the same SaaS to summarize a document. The terms are different this time: the service runs in the United States and uses an AI agent. She accepts them, but only for the file foo. The resulting root PCA grants less and constrains differently:

Each root PCA starts a distinct lineage with its own authority bound, and no later continuity advancement can expand it. These are the two lineages of Section 1.4. The continuation block in these examples is the root bootstrap challenge consumed by the first Proof of Relationship (Section 2.4). PIC Profile 0.2 carries the corresponding root challenge as challenge.next_challenge inside the signed PIC PCA COSE checkpoint.

A root PCA may be minted directly by an authenticated permissioned entity, or derived from an existing credential - for example from an OAuth access token through a profile-defined exchange. These derivations are out of scope for this specification, but they are in line with it, and one point must be clear: PIC does not change authentication. Identity and authentication mechanisms establish the origin; PIC governs only how authority propagates after that origin exists.

section.name: Prover Requirements
section.t: A PIC Prover produces the next continuity advancement for a lineage. Except for the root establishment step, every continuity advancement produced by a Prover MUST:

list.t: identify exactly one predecessor continuity state;
include or bind a cryptographic reference to that predecessor;
include or bind the relationship or executor-profile evidence required by the selected profile;
yield authority equal to or more restrictive than the predecessor materialized authority;
bind the concrete execution or request as required by the selected profile;
be integrity-protected according to the selected profile.

section.t: The first requirement is what keeps the cross-lineage composition of Section 1.4 out of the model: an advancement that combines authority from two lineages cannot be validated as a conforming continuation. An executor can always assemble arbitrary bytes locally; what it cannot do is have such a state accepted.

section.name: Conceptual Model and Logical Objects
section.t: PIC distinguishes three concepts that MUST NOT be treated as synonyms:

list.t: Proof of Possession (PoP) establishes control of a key, secret, credential, or presentation mechanism. PoP can authenticate a signer or bind a presentation, but it does not by itself establish that one execution occurrence caused or authorized another.

Proof of Relationship (PoR) is the profile-realized single-hop relation between one accepted predecessor occurrence and one proposed successor occurrence. A profile claiming full continuity MUST define the evidence, trust assumptions, and receiving predicate that soundly witness that relation.

Proof of Continuity (PoC) is the result established by a Verifier for a root and a sequence of accepted advancements when every required PoR, predecessor, freshness, integrity, non-expansion, temporal, revocation, policy, and applicable request/execution-binding check succeeds.

section.t: A field named proof_of_relationship, a valid signature, or successful PoP is evidence input, not PoC by itself. PoC is a verification result over the complete applicable acceptance predicate.

The following logical objects define the information model. They are not wire-format field names. A concrete profile MAY combine objects, encode them under different names, or replace an explicit object with a cryptographic commitment, provided the Verifier can recover or validate every semantic input required by this specification.

texttable.c: Authenticated origin, initial authority upper bound, optional execution contract, initial freshness material, validity bounds, and profile identifier. It has no predecessor and no PoR.

The accepted current lineage state: root or trusted checkpoint reference, current position or equivalent order, materialized authority, freshness state, validity bounds, and the representation's authenticated history or prior-validation commitment.

Exactly one predecessor reference, proposed successor state, PoR evidence or commitment, authority attenuation, next freshness material, temporal data, applicable request/execution binding, and integrity protection.

Profile-defined evidence from which the Verifier evaluates the concrete relation between the identified predecessor occurrence and successor occurrence. It includes or binds the successor/key/executor information required by that relation.
The materialized permissions and constraints compared under the profile's deterministic attenuation order.
An authenticated commitment to the concrete request, message, execution occurrence, or protected effect when the selected profile claims that property.

Accept or reject, the assurance level actually established, the accepted materialized authority, and the next continuity state when accepted. Diagnostic reasons are profile-defined and MUST NOT change the acceptance predicate.

section.t: A concrete profile MUST specify which representation members carry or bind these semantics, which members are integrity protected, how canonical bytes and cryptographic references are computed, and which objects are absent at the root. A profile MUST NOT rely on an unauthenticated transport field for a semantic input required by its acceptance predicate.

section.name: Prover Procedure
section.t: Given a predecessor continuity state, the Prover MUST perform the following steps and MUST NOT emit a continuity advancement if any of them fails:

list.t: validate the predecessor continuity state (Section 2.3);
establish exactly one causal predecessor;
build the relationship or executor-profile evidence required by the selected profile (Section 2.4);
keep or attenuate the predecessor materialized authority (Section 2.5);
bind the concrete execution or request as required by the selected profile;
produce the next continuity advancement artifact (Section 2.6);
ensure the resulting authority is no greater than the predecessor authority.

figure.sourcecode: receive current continuity state | v validate predecessor continuity state, or construct an untrusted candidate that a trusted receiving boundary will validate before authority is exercised | v build relationship/profile evidence and profile-required request/execution binding | v keep or attenuate materialized authority | v produce next continuity advancement | v emit updated continuity state

section.t: At the abstract level, the advancement is not required to be a PCA. The PIC Continuity Transition COSE is the proposed Profile 0.2 advancement artifact. It is carried as the single entry in transitions in a workload-signed candidate PIC Continuity COSE, which is carried by a workload-signed candidate PIC Token JWT. The trusted settlement authority validates that candidate and issues the next settled PIC Token JWT carrying a settled PIC Continuity COSE with transitions = null.

section.name: Predecessor Validation
section.t: Before treating predecessor authority as trusted or exercising it, the Prover MUST validate the predecessor continuity state by applying the Verifier procedure of Section 3. A candidate-construction library MAY parse and semantically validate a predecessor without authenticating it when all of the following hold:

list.t: the output is explicitly an untrusted candidate and is not treated as settled authority;
no protected effect is authorized from the unauthenticated parse;
the trusted receiving or settlement boundary independently performs the complete Verifier procedure before accepting the advancement;
failure at that boundary prevents issuance and authority exercise.

section.t: This exception supports profiles in which a workload lacks the trust material needed to authenticate the predecessor while constructing a candidate and a trusted receiving or settlement boundary independently revalidates that predecessor. It changes no receiving-side safety requirement.

section.name: Proof of Relationship
section.t: The abstract PoR relation binds the current execution to exactly one predecessor. A non-root advancement in a profile claiming full continuity MUST carry or cryptographically bind evidence whose concrete checks soundly witness the abstract single-hop PoR relation. A profile that validates a narrower relationship MAY define an artifact-linked assurance level, but it MUST identify the missing refinement obligation and MUST NOT claim that its evidence establishes the abstract PoR.

A proof_of_relationship field, when defined by a profile, is relationship or profile evidence. It is not by itself the complete Proof of Continuity and does not by itself establish semantic continuity. A transition is accepted as a full PIC continuation only when the required PoR relation holds and the separate non-expansion requirement, together with all other applicable profile checks such as predecessor binding, freshness, integrity, evidence or conformance, request/execution binding, revocation, and policy, also succeeds. An artifact-linked acceptance establishes only the subset its profile states.
Profile-defined concrete relationship validation may cover, as applicable:

list.t: a predecessor cryptographic reference;
challenge continuity or an equivalent profile-defined freshness mechanism;
holder, executor, or key relationship as required by the profile.

section.t: Request/execution binding and executor or execution-contract conformance remain separate applicable advancement-validation checks; they are not, merely by being required for acceptance, part of the abstract PoR relation.
For PIC Profile 0.2, the PIC Continuity Transition COSE retains the field name proof_of_relationship as a typed object:

figure.sourcecode: proof_of_relationship.type = "sd-jwt" proof_of_relationship.evidence = exact UTF-8 bytes of the textual issuer-signed Profile 0.2 SD-JWT presentation

section.t: The type value controls parsing and validation of evidence. In the current artifact-linked assurance level, this field contains executor-profile and workload-key evidence; the historical field name does not, by itself, establish the abstract relation PoR(s_i, s_{i+1}). A Profile 0.2 schema MUST bind or identify the workload verification key. This specification does not define a universal claim name and does not define a separate generic key_binding field. The predecessor reference for the current centralized Profile 0.2 realization is:

figure.sourcecode: predecessor.type = "pca" predecessor.hash = SHA-256(exact signed current root.pca PIC PCA COSE bytes)

section.t: The first transition consumes the bootstrap challenge from the current PIC PCA COSE checkpoint's challenge.next_challenge. Later transitions use the challenge.next_challenge value carried by the current signed PIC PCA COSE checkpoint. The hash input is the exact signed PIC PCA COSE artifact bytes, not a decoded payload, diagnostic notation, JSON representation, Base64url text, or reserialized structure.

The Prover MUST check the profile evidence it can validate before proceeding: if the predecessor reference does not match the predecessor continuity state, or if the challenge or equivalent freshness evidence does not satisfy the selected validation rules, the candidate is invalid and the Prover MUST stop. If profile-required executor, contract, request/execution, or other required evidence is missing or invalid, the advancement is invalid and the Prover MUST stop. The trusted Verifier MUST repeat every acceptance check independently.

What the PoR proves. The abstract PoR does not prove physical or counterfactual causation beyond the relation it models. A concrete challenge response or relationship artifact proves only the semantics defined by its selected profile. A profile MUST NOT claim the abstract single-hop PoR relation used by the model [1] and Lean formalization [2] unless it states the concrete evidence, trust assumptions, and refinement argument by which its receiving predicate soundly witnesses that relation. Executor-profile evidence and control of a bound workload key establish only those properties unless a trusted observation boundary additionally binds the concrete predecessor-to-successor occurrence.

Continuation is open by default. The core model does not require a predecessor to preselect a concrete successor. A profile MAY constrain holder keys, recipients, or channels, but those constraints are profile-specific. When a selected profile defines a request or execution commitment, that binding fixes the concrete action accepted under that profile (Section 3.3).

Out of scope. The canonical form of the request, digest construction, streaming and partial payloads, and request-binding construction are defined by the selected profile or by a separate specification. The core keeps only the profile-conditional requirement that authenticated request/execution commitments, when defined and relied upon, match the accepted or executed action (Section 3.3).

li.t: Note - proof mechanism agility. Future or separate profiles may realize PoR and advancement integrity with mechanisms other than the current Profile 0.2 typed SD-JWT evidence, including signed hash chains, Merkle proofs, accumulators, recursive or zero-knowledge proofs, or hardware-backed attestations, provided they preserve the normative semantics: binding to exactly one predecessor, profile-defined freshness or challenge continuity, non-expansion of authority, and integrity of the concrete advancement.

section.name: Invariant Monotonicity
section.t: Once the PoR holds, the Prover determines the resulting materialized authority. At each hop the authority is either kept unchanged or attenuated, never expanded:

list.t: every entry in operations MUST also be present in the predecessor operations;
every constraint of the predecessor executionContract MUST be preserved or strengthened.

section.t: A Prover MAY drop operations, add constraints, or shorten the validity period. A Prover MUST NOT add operations, relax constraints, or extend the validity period. What is dropped at a hop is lost: no later hop can reintroduce it.

For a relational execution contract, the predecessor contract governs admission of the current executor, and the successor contract must logically imply the predecessor contract: rho(i+1) => rho(i). Concrete profile evidence must be sound for the executor attributes it establishes; missing or withheld required evidence causes rejection and cannot widen admission [13].
The root authority context (Section 1.8) granted READ-ALL and BACKUP. The backup service needs only read access downstream, so it drops BACKUP and sets the attenuated invariants:
The order that decides "more restrictive" is defined by the profile (Section 4): here operations uses subset inclusion and the executionContract fields use the reference profile's order.

In PIC Profile 0.2, the PIC PCA COSE payload context_of_authority carries an Indexed Authority Map, not the normalized Logical Context of Authority directly. The logical authority shape contains optional identity_context and execution, where execution.invariants carries executable PIC authority and execution.contract carries constraints. The canonical Indexed Authority Map sections are identity_context, invariants, and execution_contract; logical execution.contract maps to execution_contract. identity_context is descriptive or contextual and does not itself grant execution authority.
Section-local numeric indexes start at 0. Bitmap identity is (section, numeric index), for example identity_context/0 or invariants/1; JSON object member order has no protocol meaning.
Indexed Authority Map entries use compact tuples. Tuple element order is normative:

list.t: identity_context: [key, value];
execution_contract: [key, value];
invariants: [scope, operation, resourceType, resourceId].

section.t: A logical Profile 0.2 execution.contract value MUST contain at least one attribute. Each logical attribute value MUST be either a non-empty string or a non-empty array of non-empty strings. Profile 0.2 implementations MUST reject logical execution.contract values containing a number, boolean, object, null, empty string, empty array, array containing an empty string, or array containing a non-string value.

Scalar logical values become one indexed tuple. Set or list membership is denormalized into independently indexed boolean membership tuples, for example ["roles:payment-approver", true]. That true is a canonical denormalized membership representation in the Indexed Authority Map; it is not permission for arbitrary boolean values in the logical execution.contract input domain. This document defines no false-valued membership semantics for Profile 0.2.

Removal attenuation applies only to attenuations.identity_context.remove_bitmap and attenuations.invariants.remove_bitmap, each evaluated against the section-local numeric indexes of its own map section. Removal never adds authority, and a removed entry cannot reappear later in the same continuity.

For Profile 0.2 removal bitmaps, byte_index = floor(i / 8), bit_index = i mod 8, and mask = 1 << bit_index; bits are interpreted least-significant-bit first. Thus index 0 is h'01', index 1 is h'02', index 2 is h'04', index 7 is h'80', and index 8 is h'0001'. A set bit referring to a nonexistent predecessor index MUST be rejected. Trailing zero bytes MUST be omitted. A no-op bitmap SHOULD be omitted together with its optional attenuation member.

Execution-contract restriction does not use a removal bitmap. Accepted restrictions are carried as attenuations.execution_contract.additions. Each proposed addition is a [key, value] tuple for the execution_contract section; the workload MUST NOT assign its numeric index. The settlement verifier validates proposed additions and assigns the next section-local numeric indexes in the materialized/effective execution_contract section. Existing execution-contract constraints are not removed, replaced, or weakened; accepted constraints accumulate with logical AND.

When one PIC Continuity Transition COSE proposes multiple execution-contract additions, the settlement verifier validates the proposed additions and denormalizes any collection-valued logical proposal material into individual canonical [key, value] additions when applicable. After denormalization, more than one accepted addition with the same canonical key MUST be rejected. The settlement verifier then sorts the remaining accepted additions lexicographically by canonical key using Unicode code point order, assigns the next section-local numeric indexes in that sorted order, and materializes the additions. Input array order MUST NOT determine materialized index assignment. The workload is not required to pre-sort the additions.

Initial PIC PCA COSE canonicalization for Profile 0.2 is deterministic. Implementations denormalize the Logical Context of Authority into canonical tuple candidates, sort candidates within each section, and then assign section-local numeric indexes starting at 0.

For identity_context and execution_contract, candidates are sorted lexicographically by canonical key, using Unicode code point order. Collection memberships are denormalized before sorting; each member becomes its own [key, true] tuple, and the complete resulting canonical membership key determines ordering. For invariants, candidates are sorted lexicographically by tuple elements in this order: scope, operation, resourceType, resourceId, using Unicode code point order for each element. After sorting, indexes 0, 1, 2, and so on are assigned within each section. Implementations MUST NOT derive index values from JSON object member order.

Canonical serialization of an already indexed Profile 0.2 authority map is separate from initial index assignment. For serialization and authority-state structural ordering, sections are ordered as identity_context, invariants, execution_contract, and entries within each indexed section are ordered by ascending numeric index. This ordering defines the deterministic canonical structure, but does not by itself define an interoperable hash-input byte string. An authority-state hash, when defined by a selected profile or schema, requires that profile or schema to define the exact byte serialization used as hash input. Profile 0.2 signed-artifact references such as root.pca_hash and predecessor.hash are computed over exact signed COSE artifact bytes. Authority-state identity and signed-artifact identity are separate domains.

section.name: Continuity Advancement Construction
section.t: The Prover assembles the next continuity advancement from the PoR of Section 2.4, the attenuation of Section 2.5, the request or execution binding required by the profile, and the profile-defined freshness material for the next step. The profile defines the signed artifact that protects those values.

In PIC Profile 0.2, a PIC Continuity Transition COSE contains position, a structured predecessor reference, challenge.previous_challenge, challenge.next_challenge, optional attenuations, and typed proof_of_relationship. It is carried only by the workload-produced candidate PIC Continuity COSE for the current exchange. The settlement authority validates the candidate and, if the advancement is accepted, issues the next settled PIC Token JWT carrying a settled PIC Continuity COSE with transitions = null. Diagnostic JSON-like or CBOR-like views are illustrative unless a selected profile assigns exact encodings.
The following non-normative sketch shows the abstract contents of an advancement:

The integrity protection MUST cover the predecessor reference, PoR, attenuation, freshness material, temporal fields, and any request/execution binding required by the selected profile. A valid signature or proof is necessary but not sufficient: the Verifier still performs all semantic checks in Section 3.

section.name: Worked End-to-End Example
section.t: This subsection is non-normative. It shows the logical objects and ordered decision for one complete hop. The JSON member names and example values are explanatory only; they do not assign a JSON wire format, registered claim names, or cryptographic suite.
The trusted root state S0 grants READ and BACKUP and supplies freshness material for its first successor:

The Prover proposes candidate T1. It identifies only S0, drops BACKUP, binds the request occurrence, answers the predecessor freshness value, and supplies the relationship evidence required by the example profile:
The Verifier accepts this candidate only after all of the following are true:

list.t: S0 is an authenticated, unexpired predecessor trusted under the selected profile;
the predecessor reference in T1 resolves to exactly S0;
the concrete relationship predicate validates the evidence for occurrence 91b2 and soundly witnesses the profile's PoR;
the freshness response equals the value issued by S0, and the next freshness value satisfies the profile;
the successor key or executor evidence satisfies the predecessor execution contract;
the authenticated request digest equals the digest of the request accepted or executed at the enforcement boundary;
{READ} is no more permissive than {READ, BACKUP}, and the execution contract is preserved or strengthened;
the candidate satisfies integrity, time, revocation, and applicable policy checks.

section.t: Only after those checks may the Verifier return an accepted next state:
The following variants MUST be rejected by a profile claiming the corresponding property:

texttable.c: The candidate is correctly signed, but its evidence proves only control of successorKey.
PoP is not PoR; the causal relationship is not established.
successor.authority.operations is ["READ", "DELETE"].
DELETE expands authority beyond S0.
previousChallenge differs from the challenge in S0, or reuses material outside the profile's permitted consumption semantics.
Freshness or challenge continuity fails.
The concrete request digest differs from requestBinding.digest.
Request/execution binding fails.
The candidate imports authority from another lineage or identifies more than one ordinary predecessor.
Single-lineage, exactly-one-predecessor continuity fails.
Relationship evidence is valid but the executor is agentic.
The predecessor's deterministic execution contract is not satisfied.

section.t: An artifact-linked profile may accept a narrower candidate only for the properties its predicate actually verifies. It MUST NOT label that result full-continuity or claim PoC over an observed handoff or request occurrence that it did not authenticate.

section.name: Verifier Requirements
section.t: A PIC Verifier validates a continuity state before any authority is exercised. The checks are profile-dependent in representation but not in semantics. A Verifier MUST:

list.t: establish and validate the trusted root;
validate the concrete continuity representation selected by the profile;
validate every required causal advancement or equivalent proof representation;
materialize the current authority;
accept only if every required check succeeds; otherwise reject.

section.t: The authority a Verifier may authorize at the current hop is the current materialized authority. By monotonicity (Section 2.5), it is bounded by the root authority, so a privilege absent from the root cannot be authorized downstream.

section.name: Verifier Procedure
section.t: Given a received continuity state, the Verifier MUST perform the following steps and MUST reject the hop if any of them fails:

list.t: establish the trusted root authority representation;
validate the root representation and its authenticated origin;
validate the profile-selected continuity representation;
validate predecessor continuity for each required advancement;
validate the relationship/profile evidence required for each non-root advancement and, when full PoR is claimed, validate the concrete predicate that witnesses the abstract PoR;
validate challenge continuity or the equivalent freshness mechanism used by the profile;
validate profile-required evidence, conformance, freshness, temporal state, and revocation state;
validate request/execution binding when required by the selected profile, and do not claim that property when no authenticated occurrence or request commitment is available;
apply profile-defined attenuations and verify non-expansion;
verify the final materialized authority commitment when the profile defines one;
accept the materialized current authority.

section.t: For PIC Profile 0.2, ordinary verification of a settled artifact includes verifying the settled PIC Token JWT signature, obtaining pic.root as the exact PIC Continuity COSE bytes, verifying the settled PIC Continuity COSE signature and profile, verifying that transitions = null, verifying root.pca as the exact signed PIC PCA COSE bytes for the current trusted checkpoint, recomputing root.pca_hash, and verifying that the signed PIC PCA COSE payload supplies the materialized authority, position, and challenge.next_challenge. When lineage_id or expires_at is present in that checkpoint, a binding that mirrors those values into PIC Token JWT jti or exp MUST validate equality and MUST NOT extend the checkpoint lifetime. When revocation is enabled for a revocable continuity, the Verifier also validates the authenticated revocation coordinates required by the PIC Revocation Specification before evaluating applicable authenticated revocation state. The base Profile 0.2 artifact schema does not assign one universal PCA-ID mapping. A revocation binding MAY select the signed PCA lineage_id as its stable lineage/PCA identifier and mirror it into JWT jti, while PCA position supplies path depth. Ordinary Profile 0.2 Verifiers are not required to replay a transported transition history.
When a trusted settlement authority processes a Profile 0.2 advancement candidate, it additionally:

list.t: receives the candidate PIC Token JWT as untrusted input and parses it without accepting authenticity;
obtains pic.root as untrusted candidate PIC Continuity COSE bytes;
parses the candidate Continuity without accepting authenticity and validates the presence and shape of root.pca, root.pca_hash, and transitions;
requires transitions to contain exactly one PIC Continuity Transition COSE;
parses that Transition as untrusted input and extracts proof_of_relationship;
validates the proof_of_relationship structure, treating the field name as a Profile 0.2 compatibility name rather than proof that the abstract PoR has been discharged;
requires proof_of_relationship.type = "sd-jwt";
parses proof_of_relationship.evidence as the exact UTF-8 bytes of the textual issuer-signed Profile 0.2 SD-JWT presentation;
validates the SD-JWT issuer signature, issuer trust, required disclosures, claims, validity interval, and schema requirements;
obtains or resolves the workload verification key accepted from the profile evidence;
recomputes SHA-256(exact signed root.pca PIC PCA COSE bytes) and compares it with root.pca_hash;
verifies that Transition.position = current PCA.position + 1;
verifies predecessor.type = "pca" and predecessor.hash = SHA-256(exact signed current root.pca PIC PCA COSE bytes);
verifies that Transition.challenge.previous_challenge = current PCA.challenge.next_challenge, requires a non-empty challenge.next_challenge, and requires that it differ from previous_challenge;
validates removal bitmaps and execution-contract additions, including deterministic ordering and section-local index assignment for accepted additions;

validates request/execution binding and executor evidence or conformance when required by the selected profile; a deployment with no authenticated request or occurrence commitment MUST treat request binding as unsupported rather than satisfied;
validates authority non-expansion, revocation, and local/profile policy;

materializes the new authority, creates logical PCA N+1, transfers the accepted next challenge into it, serializes and signs it as a new PIC PCA COSE checkpoint, creates a settled PIC Continuity COSE with the new root.pca, recomputed root.pca_hash, and transitions = null, and creates/signs the settled PIC Token JWT.

section.t: If validation succeeds, the settlement authority issues the next settled PIC Token JWT. A settlement implementation that lacks a trusted runtime occurrence or authenticated request to compare with request_digest establishes only the artifact-linked subset of these checks and MUST NOT claim request binding or observed-handoff PoR.

section.name: Root Validation
section.t: The root authority context is validated differently from later advancements: it carries no Proof of Relationship and no predecessor reference, because there is no predecessor. The Verifier MUST:

list.t: verify the root representation according to the selected profile;
verify that the root issuer or origin authority is trusted for the represented authority;
confirm applicable temporal and revocation state;
extract the root authority and any root bootstrap challenge or equivalent freshness material.

section.t: In PIC Profile 0.2, the root representation is the signed PIC PCA COSE checkpoint carried as exact bytes in root.pca by the settled PIC Continuity COSE. The PIC PCA COSE carries the Indexed Authority Map, position = 0, and challenge.next_challenge, which initializes the first PIC Continuity Transition COSE. The signed-artifact hash is carried as root.pca_hash and is computed over the exact signed PIC PCA COSE bytes.

section.name: Advancement Validation
section.t: For each non-root continuity advancement, the Verifier MUST perform the following checks and MUST reject the continuity state if any fails:

list.t: integrity — the advancement artifact or proof is valid under the profile's canonical encoding and cryptographic suite (Section 7.4);

predecessor binding — the predecessor cryptographic reference identifies exactly one predecessor continuity state, and the challenge answered, authority attenuated, and execution contract checked all belong to that same predecessor;
continuation — the challenge or equivalent freshness mechanism satisfies the selected profile and has the declared consumption scope (Section 7.1);
executor / relationship evidence — when required by the selected profile, the required executor, holder, key, attestation, or equivalent relationship evidence is valid according to that profile;
non-expansion — the resulting authority is equal to or more restrictive than the predecessor materialized authority under the profile's attenuation order (Section 4);
temporal — the advancement and resulting continuity state satisfy the profile's temporal rules (Section 7.3);

request/execution binding — when the selected profile defines or requires a request/execution commitment, the concrete action accepted or executed matches the operation, target, parameters, digests, or equivalent semantic values bound by that commitment.

section.t: A valid signature establishes integrity, not semantic validity: checks 2–8 are separate and the Verifier MUST NOT skip them because the signature verified. The Verifier does not trust that the Prover already performed these checks; it repeats them independently.

Executed-vs-bound. When a selected profile defines a request/execution commitment and relies on that commitment to authorize a concrete action, the reference monitor or equivalent enforcement point MUST ensure that the action accepted or executed matches the authenticated commitment. Signing or binding one action and executing another is invalid under that profile.

This is where the cross-lineage composition of Section 1.4 fails: authority absent from the predecessor fails non-expansion (6), and a PoR that does not bind to the predecessor fails continuation (3) or predecessor binding (2). Such a state cannot be validated as a conforming continuation, even though an executor can always assemble arbitrary bytes locally.

section.name: Authority as an Abstract Domain
section.t: PIC does not define the application's authorization vocabulary and does not replace its access-control system. It preserves the causal continuity and non-expansion of an authority context whose meaning is defined by the application or by an applicable PIC profile. That context may be represented as operation-resource pairs, roles, labels, scopes (for example lifted from an OAuth token), capability classes, or policy references. Normatively the requirement is only:

figure.sourcecode: authority(i+1) ≤ authority(i)

section.t: where ≤ is an attenuation order defined by the profile. The operations set with subset inclusion, used in the examples, is the reference profile: it corresponds to the operation-resource privileges of the model [1].

A label may denote authority without listing it: EU-BACKUP-READONLY denotes a set of operation-resource permissions and carries that meaning by reference. This preserves the authority non-expansion premise rather than discarding it: a label is defined to denote a semantic set (in the reference case an O×R set), and the label order is required to refine the subset order on those denotations. O×R is thus the profile where non-expansion is immediate, and any other profile inherits that premise exactly to the extent that its order refines its denotation order. The full confused-deputy result still requires the separate PoR, causal-attribution, and mediation assumptions stated in Section 7.5.

section.name: Attenuation Profiles
section.t: Every profile that introduces an authority representation MUST define its syntax, its equivalence relation, its attenuation order ≤, and a deterministic comparison sufficient for non-expansion validation.

A profile that uses an execution contract MUST additionally define the conformance semantics or function required to determine whether presented executor evidence satisfies that contract, when the profile requires such conformance evidence. For example:

figure.sourcecode: role: current == predecessor allowedRegions: current ⊆ predecessor requiredCompliance: current ⊇ predecessor executionModel: current ⊆ predecessor expiresAt: current ≤ predecessor

section.t: The core uses the abstract relation Attenuates(current, predecessor, profile); a Verifier MUST reject a PCA whose profile is unknown or does not define a deterministic comparison. Concrete profiles for specific domains are defined by separate specifications. Translation between heterogeneous authority domains is out of scope here; consistent with the model, an overly permissive translation is a profile error, not a violation of the continuity invariant.

section.name: Policy Decision Point (PDP) Integration
section.t: PIC and access control answer different questions:

figure.sourcecode: PIC: is this authority state a valid non-expansive continuation of the state that caused the execution? Access control: does this authority state authorize this concrete operation under the application policy?

section.t: Using a PDP is an application choice, not part of PIC. An executor MAY evaluate policy locally, or it MAY pass the authority context to a Policy Decision Point — Cedar, Rego, XACML, or another engine — that interprets the label's semantics and renders the access decision. The two decisions MAY run in one component or in separate ones. PIC neither requires a PDP nor defines one; this section exists only for implementers who choose that path.

Whoever takes that path takes an obligation with it, and it is theirs, not PIC's: the declared attenuation order on labels MUST be monotone with respect to their semantics. If current ≤ predecessor in the label order but the meaning of current is not contained in the meaning of predecessor, PIC's non-expansion is vacuous — the labels shrink while what they authorize grows. Establishing that the label order refines its denotation order is up to the application or its PDP. It does not inherit the Lean proof [2]: the proof covers non-expansion of the abstract order only; semantic monotonicity of a concrete vocabulary is a separate proof obligation that PIC does not discharge. This is the same boundary the model already draws for heterogeneous translation, and it is a natural point of standardization — label vocabularies with provably semantic-monotone orders, and the PIC↔PDP interface that carries the obligation.

section.name: Continuity Representations
section.t: A PIC continuity state can be represented and validated in more than one way. The choice does not change the model - the invariants and the checks of Section 3 stay the same - but it changes validation cost and trust assumptions. This section contains non-normative representation guidance and explicit profile requirements. A representation does not inherit the Lean proof automatically. A profile claiming full PIC continuity MUST show that its concrete acceptance predicate implies the abstract PoC (Section 7.5). A partial implementation MAY expose a narrower assurance level only when it names the verified subset and the missing refinement obligations, and it MUST NOT label that result a Proof of Continuity or full PIC conformance.
A continuity profile MAY use:

list.t: self-contained transition graphs;
incremental representations;
compacted or checkpointed representations;
referenced history;
succinct proofs;
other proof mechanisms.

section.t: The profile MUST define its acceptance predicate, canonicalization, cryptographic references, freshness mechanism, authority materialization, and failure behavior. A full-continuity profile MUST preserve exactly-one-predecessor continuity, PoR, non-expansion, request/execution binding when required by that profile, and verifier independence. A partial assurance level MUST preserve every property it claims and MUST fail closed for every check declared mandatory at that level.

section.name: Current Profile 0.2 Representation
section.t: PIC Profile 0.2 uses centralized settlement. A settled PIC Token JWT is issued by the trusted settlement authority and carries a settled PIC Continuity COSE in pic.root. That Continuity carries the exact signed PIC PCA COSE bytes for the current trusted checkpoint in root.pca, the matching root.pca_hash, and transitions = null. root.pca is the current checkpoint, not an immutable genesis artifact: after an accepted advancement it changes from PIC PCA COSE N to PIC PCA COSE N+1.

figure.sourcecode:
trusted settled PIC Token JWT N `-- pic.root = settled PIC Continuity COSE N +-- root.pca = exact signed PIC PCA COSE N bytes +-- root.pca_hash = SHA-256(exact signed PIC PCA COSE N bytes) `-- transitions = null
workload-signed candidate PIC Token JWT `-- pic.root = workload-signed candidate PIC Continuity COSE +-- root.pca = exact signed PIC PCA COSE N bytes +-- root.pca_hash = matching SHA-256 digest `-- transitions = [ exactly one workload-signed PIC Continuity Transition COSE N+1 ]
trusted settlement validation
trusted settled PIC Token JWT N+1 `-- pic.root = settled PIC Continuity COSE N+1 +-- root.pca = exact signed PIC PCA COSE N+1 bytes +-- root.pca_hash = SHA-256(exact signed PIC PCA COSE N+1 bytes) `-- transitions = null

section.t: The candidate is not a trusted settled continuity artifact. The settlement authority validates the current settled continuity, the candidate PIC Token JWT, the candidate PIC Continuity COSE, the single PIC Continuity Transition COSE, profile/key evidence, predecessor hash over the exact current PIC PCA COSE bytes, position increment, challenge continuity, removal attenuations, execution-contract additions including deterministic canonical ordering and index assignment for accepted additions, non-expansion, revocation, and local/profile policy. If validation succeeds, the settlement authority materializes the new authority into a new PIC PCA COSE checkpoint and issues the next settled PIC Token JWT.

Profile 0.2 does not transport a replayable transition graph in the settled PIC Continuity COSE. The current authority and post-initial challenge material are represented by the latest trusted PIC PCA COSE checkpoint carried in root.pca; the settled Continuity itself has no position field and no challenge field.

section.name: Profile 0.2 Assurance Boundary
section.t: The abstract PIC Model and the base Profile 0.2 artifact predicate have different claim boundaries. A conforming document or implementation MUST identify which boundary it is claiming. The artifact-linked level is a partial assurance class, not an alternative definition of PoR and not full PIC conformance.

texttable.c: Signed artifact lineage and exactly-one predecessor reference
Required
Authority attenuation and irreversible branch-local removal
Required
Additive execution-contract refinement and executor-profile conformance
Required when that evidence schema is selected
Trusted-issuer executor-profile evidence and workload-key binding
Required by the base SD-JWT evidence binding
Unknown successor and sibling fan-out
Permitted intentionally
Stable lineage correlation and absolute lineage expiry
Required when the corresponding optional fields are selected by a binding
Abstract semantic PoR(s_i, s_{i+1}) for an observed handoff occurrence
Not established by the base artifact predicate
Authenticated request or runtime-occurrence binding
Profile-defined; not established when absent
Global single consumption or exactly-once execution
Not defined by the base artifact predicate
Per-lineage early revocation
Defined only by a selected revocation binding
Complete mediation and causal attribution of protected actions
Deployment and profile obligations outside artifact settlement alone

section.t: The resulting base assurance level is called artifact-linked. It is valid to claim that a conforming artifact verifier excludes authority import from an unrelated lineage within an accepted artifact transition and enforces the selected executor profile. It is not valid to infer from that claim that a trusted boundary observed the physical or runtime handoff, that a particular request caused the candidate, or that every protected effect passed through settlement.

A future profile may claim full semantic PoR only after defining authenticated occurrence evidence, the trusted observer and its failure model, request or message binding where applicable, verification and retention rules, and a refinement argument from its concrete acceptance predicate to the abstract relation used by the formal model. Adding another workload-self-asserted field does not by itself provide that refinement [13].

section.name: Profile 0.2 Artifact Semantics
section.t: This subsection is normative for PIC Profile 0.2. The semantic field names below are normative for this profile. Exact CBOR integer labels, COSE protected-header typ values, media-type registrations, and any IANA assignments are deferred to the applicable profile registry or a later byte-level wire assignment; this subsection does not invent them.
The active PIC Profile 0.2 identifier is:

figure.sourcecode: https://pic-protocol.org/profiles/0.2

section.t: Profile 0.2 uses the following artifact format identifiers:

texttable.c: PIC Token JWT
PIC PCA COSE
PIC Continuity COSE
PIC Continuity Transition COSE

section.t: These identifiers are Profile 0.2 format identifiers, not IANA-assigned media types unless and until a registration assigns that status.
Profile 0.2 also uses the following stable semantic definition URIs:

texttable.c: PIC Token type URI
Initial Continuity Proposal type URI

section.name: PIC Token JWT
section.t: A PIC Token JWT has format identifier pic+jwt.
The pic.root member MUST contain the unpadded Base64url encoding of the exact binary PIC Continuity COSE artifact bytes.

A candidate PIC Token JWT is workload-signed. A settled PIC Token JWT is signed by the trusted settlement authority. Candidate and settled tokens use the same pic+jwt format; no second token format is defined for the candidate role. Profile 0.2 requires JOSE typ = "pic+jwt" and a profile claim equal to https://pic-protocol.org/profiles/0.2.
PIC Token JWT may carry the standard claims iss, sub, aud, iat, exp, and jti. When a Profile 0.2 binding selects stable lineage correlation and absolute lineage expiration:

list.t: every initialized lineage has a non-empty PCA lineage_id and a positive PCA expires_at;
settled and candidate JWT jti MUST equal that lineage_id;
settled and candidate JWT exp MUST equal that expires_at;
advancement MUST preserve both PCA values unchanged and MUST NOT mint a later expiration;
the settlement authority MUST reject a candidate whose jti or exp is missing or mismatched, or whose predecessor has expired.

section.t: These bindings provide stable correlation and prevent lifetime extension. They do not by themselves establish request binding or semantic PoR.

section.name: PIC PCA COSE
section.t: A PIC PCA COSE is the signed checkpoint artifact representing a logical PCA. Its Profile 0.2 semantic payload contains:

figure.sourcecode: profile lineage_id optional; a selected binding may require it expires_at optional; a selected binding may require it position context_of_authority challenge.next_challenge

section.t: position is a non-negative canonical integer defined by Profile 0.2. context_of_authority is the canonical Indexed Authority Map defined in Section 2.5. challenge.next_challenge is non-empty binary challenge material for the next Profile 0.2 transition. lineage_id, when present, is a non-empty stable identifier preserved by every advancement. expires_at, when present, is a positive NumericDate preserved by every advancement. A binding that requires both fields mirrors them into JWT jti and exp as described above.

section.name: PIC Continuity COSE
section.t: A PIC Continuity COSE has the following Profile 0.2 semantic payload:

figure.sourcecode: profile root: pca_hash pca transitions

section.t: root.pca MUST contain the exact signed PIC PCA COSE bytes for the current trusted checkpoint. root.pca_hash MUST equal SHA-256(exact signed root.pca bytes), and Verifiers MUST recompute it.

A settled Profile 0.2 Continuity MUST have transitions = null. A candidate Profile 0.2 Continuity MUST have transitions containing exactly one PIC Continuity Transition COSE. PIC Continuity COSE itself does not require a position field or challenge field in Profile 0.2; those values belong to PIC PCA COSE checkpoints and PIC Continuity Transition COSE artifacts.

section.name: PIC Continuity Transition COSE
section.t: A PIC Continuity Transition COSE has the following Profile 0.2 semantic payload:

figure.sourcecode: profile position predecessor: type hash challenge: previous_challenge next_challenge attenuations optional proof_of_relationship: type evidence request_digest optional/profile-defined executor_evidence optional/profile-defined

section.t: For current Profile 0.2, predecessor.type MUST be "pca" and predecessor.hash MUST equal SHA-256(exact signed current root.pca PIC PCA COSE bytes). A future or separate profile MAY define another predecessor representation while preserving exactly-one-predecessor semantics.

position MUST equal the predecessor PCA position plus one. challenge.previous_challenge MUST equal the predecessor PCA challenge.next_challenge. Both challenge values MUST be non-empty. The Profile 0.2 transition requires challenge.next_challenge != challenge.previous_challenge; this prevents a successor checkpoint from retaining the challenge answered by the transition. It is challenge-state progress, not global single-consumption: valid sibling candidates from one predecessor remain permitted, and replay or exactly-once effect control remains a separate property.

proof_of_relationship is a typed object. For current Profile 0.2, proof_of_relationship.type MUST be "sd-jwt" and proof_of_relationship.evidence MUST be a byte string containing the exact UTF-8 bytes of the textual issuer-signed SD-JWT presentation selected by the Profile 0.2 evidence schema. That schema MUST bind or identify the workload verification key used to verify the workload-signed candidate artifacts. The Profile 0.2 SD-JWT evidence binding obtains the workload key from disclosed cnf.jwk, rejects SD-JWT presentations carrying a separate key-binding JWT, validates the configured issuer signature and trust, disclosure integrity and uniqueness, credential validity, and algorithm compatibility, and requires the candidate JWT, Continuity COSE, and Transition COSE signatures to match that key. A separate evidence binding may define a different authenticated claim path without changing the base artifact schema, but it MUST define a distinct binding identifier and complete validation procedure.
Signer roles are:

figure.sourcecode:
PoR issuer signs issuer-signed SD-JWT
workload key accepted through profile evidence signs PIC Continuity Transition COSE signs candidate PIC Continuity COSE signs candidate PIC Token JWT
trusted settlement authority signs new PIC PCA COSE signs settled PIC Continuity COSE signs settled PIC Token JWT

section.t: The candidate Continuity COSE and Transition COSE MUST declare algorithms compatible with the accepted workload key, and their protected-header key identifiers MUST match. The candidate JWT JOSE algorithm MUST be compatible with the same key. Algorithm labels and key identifiers are inputs to verification; a valid signature under a different declared algorithm or inconsistent candidate signer metadata MUST be rejected.

The workload signatures prove control of the selected workload key and authenticate the candidate objects. The SD-JWT proves only the issuer-authenticated profile claims and key binding selected by its schema. Neither fact, alone or together, proves an observed handoff or request occurrence; the Verifier still performs the complete Profile 0.2 validation procedure and reports only the assurance level it actually establishes.

section.name: Profile 0.2 OAuth Token Exchange Binding
section.t: OAuth is not required by the PIC model. This subsection is normative only for a Profile 0.2 binding that uses OAuth Token Exchange [7] as an entry or advancement transport.
For initialization:

grant_type urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:token-exchange
subject_token OAuth access token
subject_token_type urn:ietf:params:oauth:token-type:access_token
requested_token_type https://pic-protocol.org/definitions/token-types/pic
continuity_proposal compact UTF-8 JSON encoded with unpadded Base64url; the decoded object is self-describing and has type https://pic-protocol.org/definitions/proposal-types/continuity-initial
result settlement-authority-signed settled PIC Token JWT 0

section.t: For PIC-to-PIC advancement:

figure.sourcecode:
grant_type urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:token-exchange
subject_token workload-signed candidate PIC Token JWT
subject_token_type https://pic-protocol.org/definitions/token-types/pic
requested_token_type https://pic-protocol.org/definitions/token-types/pic

result settlement-authority-signed settled PIC Token JWT N+1

section.t: The initialization proposal is interpreted by its internal type member. Profile 0.2 PIC-to-PIC advancement MUST omit continuity_proposal; the exchange binding MUST reject an advancement request that supplies it.

The RFC 8693 response MAY transport the returned PIC Token JWT in the access_token response member. That placement does not make the PIC Token JWT an OAuth Bearer token. For this Profile 0.2 binding, when an issued_token_type response member is returned for a PIC Token JWT, its value is https://pic-protocol.org/definitions/token-types/pic. When a token_type response member is returned for a PIC Token JWT, its value is "N_A".

Endpoint paths, client authentication, and the complete Initial Continuity Proposal schema are defined by the selected exchange binding. This document does not assign additional OAuth endpoint paths, client-authentication rules, proposal schema fields, or URI values beyond the Profile 0.2 identifiers above.

section.name: Profile 0.2 Failure Behavior
section.t: A settlement implementation MUST fail closed when any required parsing, signature, trust, predecessor, challenge, attenuation, conformance, temporal, revocation, or policy check fails, and MUST NOT issue a successor checkpoint from a rejected candidate.

When Profile 0.2 advancement is transported through the OAuth Token Exchange binding above, a candidate-validation refusal MUST be reported as OAuth invalid_grant and MAY include a human-readable error_description. This version does not define stable machine-readable subcodes for individual Verifier checks. Implementations and conformance vectors MUST NOT treat prose descriptions as stable reason identifiers. A later binding may define stable refusal codes without changing the acceptance predicate.

section.name: Self-Contained Transition Graphs
section.t: A future or separate profile MAY use a self-contained transition graph, provided the profile defines the graph format, predecessor references, authority materialization, proof requirements, and acceptance predicate. A graph whose ordinary nodes retain the core exactly-one-predecessor rule represents forks as separate paths. A causal-DAG profile that permits ordinary multi-parent nodes MUST enforce the every-parent bound described in Section 1.4; non-conservative joins require an explicit authorized composition or relaxation rule. Such a graph is not the current Profile 0.2 realization.

section.name: Incremental, Checkpointed, or Referenced History
section.t: A profile MAY carry only the information needed for the receiving Verifier, rely on external authenticated state, use checkpoints, use compacted or referenced history, or combine those mechanisms. Such a profile MUST define what the Verifier independently verifies and what trust assumption, if any, is placed on a validator, checkpoint issuer, history service, or prior verifier.

section.name: Succinct Proofs
section.t: The validity of a continuity prefix can be represented by a succinct proof - for example a zero-knowledge proof or accumulator proof - that a Verifier checks without walking the entire prefix. The choice of construction, soundness assumptions, setup, disclosure properties, and verification procedure are out of scope for this document and MUST be defined by the selected profile.

section.name: Conformance Requirements
section.t: This subsection is normative. A conformance claim MUST identify the exact version of this document, the selected profile and profile version, the claimed role or roles, and the assurance level actually established.

list.t: A Prover-conformant implementation MUST satisfy the Prover procedure and produce every semantic input required by the selected profile.

A Verifier-conformant implementation MUST perform the complete applicable Verifier procedure independently, reject on every mandatory check failure, and authorize no authority broader than the accepted materialized authority.

A full-continuity claim MUST document how the concrete acceptance predicate refines the abstract PoR and non-expansion predicates and MUST identify the trusted observation, request-binding, causal-completeness, and mediation assumptions on which any protected-effect claim depends.

An artifact-linked or other partial claim MUST enumerate the properties established and the refinement obligations not established. It MUST NOT describe the result as PoC, full PIC continuity, or the full PIC confused-deputy exclusion result.

A profile-conformant implementation MUST use the profile's canonical encoding, algorithms, object bindings, evidence validation, attenuation order, freshness semantics, temporal rules, revocation behavior, and failure behavior without undocumented substitution.

section.t: An interoperable profile SHOULD publish deterministic positive and negative conformance vectors. At minimum, its vector set should cover:

section.name: Origins, Authorship, and Historical Record
section.t: This section is informative and is included so that the document preserves its provenance when distributed independently.

The Provenance Identity Continuity (PIC) Model was originally developed by Nicola Gallo as a formal framework for reasoning about causal authority propagation across distributed execution. Its development introduced Proof of Relationship (PoR), Proof of Continuity (PoC), authority non-expansion, relational attenuation, and event-level causal provenance as connected parts of the framework. The PIC Specifications translate those formal results into technical requirements and are published and maintained by Nitro Agility S.r.l. as Specification Steward.
